answer.label: Not John D. Rockefeller — anonymous 1925 advertising copy
answer.authorDates: Phrase first documented April 1925 · Cleveland, Ohio
answer.sourceLine: There is no documented source in which Rockefeller says this. Quote Investigator finds its earliest close match in an advertisement for The Equity Savings & Loan Company printed in the Cleveland Plain Dealer on 27 April 1925 — “The Eighth Wonder of the World—is compound interest” — carrying no attribution at all, and hypothesises that an unknown advertising copywriter wrote it. QI states plainly that it has found no substantive evidence that Einstein, Baron Rothschild or John D. Rockefeller employed the saying.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “The Eighth Wonder of the World—is compound interest. It does things to money. At the Equity it doubles your money every 14 years…”
trail: Quote Investigator’s earliest close match is an advertisement for The Equity Savings & Loan Company in the Cleveland Plain Dealer of 27 April 1925: “The Eighth Wonder of the World—is compound interest.” QI notes that no attribution was specified, and hypothesises the line was crafted by an unknown advertising copywriter and later reassigned to famous people to make it sound more impressive.

The only Rockefeller credit in QI’s chronology is dated 14 October 1981: a guest column by Robert Lindwall in the Herald-Times-Reporter of Manitowoc, Wisconsin, which credited “Old Grandpa Rockerfeller… the multi-millionaire who preached thrift.” QI observes that the description matches the business magnate, though the odd spelling might be an allusion to an old person’s “rocker.”

Rockefeller’s own memoir offers no support: a full-text search of Project Gutenberg’s edition of Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909) returns no occurrence of “compound” and none of “eighth wonder.”
Wikiquote’s John D. Rockefeller page keeps both a Disputed and a Misattributed section, and the compound-interest line appears in neither — it is not on the page at all.
source.excerptNote: This is the 1925 bank advertisement, not Rockefeller. It ran with no attribution while Rockefeller was still alive, and the words are the copywriter’s; the tidier modern sentence — “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world” — is a later smoothing of it.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording, because it has no identifiable author. The nearest documented ancestor is an anonymous newspaper advertisement of 27 April 1925 — that specific ad text, published in the United States before 1931, would itself be public domain — but the popular Rockefeller-credited sentence is not the 1925 wording and has no traceable first publication of its own.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: About John D. Rockefeller
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller Sr. (8 July 1839 – 23 May 1937) was an American businessman and philanthropist who built the Standard Oil Company into a company controlling roughly 90% of United States oil refining by 1900, until the Supreme Court broke it up in 1911. He then gave away some $530 million, founding the University of Chicago, Rockefeller University and, in 1913, the Rockefeller Foundation. Because his name is shorthand for accumulated wealth and personal thrift, financial slogans gravitate to him — which is how an anonymous savings-and-loan advertisement ended up wearing his signature.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “celebrity upgrade”: anonymous savings-and-loan ad copy that kept acquiring more impressive authors as it travelled. Quote Investigator documents at least three claimants, and finds evidence for none of them.

items.why: QI found no substantive evidence Rockefeller employed the saying. The only Rockefeller credit in its chronology is a guest column in the Herald-Times-Reporter of Manitowoc, Wisconsin, dated 14 October 1981 — forty-four years after Rockefeller’s death in 1937 — and it names him only as “Old Grandpa Rockerfeller.”

A 1965 advertisement in The Wall Street Journal, placed by the Community Savings and Loan Association of Compton, California, asked readers what Baron Rothschild considered the eighth wonder of the world. QI points out that there have been multiple Barons Rothschild, so the name is ambiguous — and finds no evidence any of them said it.

The Einstein credit surfaces later still: a 1988 personal-finance column in the Courier-Post quoted a financial analyst invoking “Albert Einstein’s remark.” Princeton University Press’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein files the saying under “Probably Not By Einstein,” as QI records.

misattribution.truthLine: The phrase started as unattributed 1925 bank advertising and picked up its famous bylines decades afterwards; QI found no substantive evidence that Rockefeller, Rothschild or Einstein ever used it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The arithmetic behind the line is real, which is why nobody ever stops to check it. What the famous byline adds is authority: a savings pitch becomes received wisdom the moment a tycoon appears to have signed it. Advertisers were already fluent in this move — QI shows the “Eighth Wonder of the World” label attached to an 1816 English bridge lottery, an 1853 patent elixir, the Brooklyn Bridge in 1883, and, in 1911, a trick Shetland pony named Cupid.

Rockefeller is an unusually convenient host for it. He was the era’s emblem of accumulated money and, as the 1981 columnist put it, a multi-millionaire who preached thrift — so a thrift slogan sticks to him without friction. Tellingly, when the M.I.T. economist Paul Samuelson used the phrase in a February 1967 column, he wrote of “what has been called the eighth wonder of the world—compound interest,” crediting nobody. In 1967 it was still a floating proverb, not a quotation.
detailsBody: Even the single source behind the Rockefeller version is loose. The 1981 Manitowoc column does not cite a speech, a book or a letter; it reports a remembered saying by “Old Grandpa Rockerfeller,” a spelling QI suggests may be a pun on an old person’s “rocker” rather than a considered reference to the oil magnate.

A neighbouring claim follows the same pattern. QI’s companion article on “compound interest is man’s greatest invention” traces that saying to a 1916 advertisement for the Security Investment Company in a Riverside, California newspaper, and finds it very unlikely Einstein said it either.
context.pull: Ad copy first. Famous byline decades later.
